snippet.title: NBA Jam T.E. Longplay (PlayStation Version) - Difficulty: 5 (Extra Hard)
snippet.description:
- NBA Jam T.E. Longplay (PlayStation Version) - Difficulty: 5 (Extra Hard) -

NBA Jam Tournament Edition is an arcade basketball game developed by Midway and originally released in arcades in 1994. Rather than reinventing NBA Jam, Tournament Edition takes the original game's enormously successful two-on-two formula and expands it with larger rosters, more options, additional players and an even greater emphasis on exaggerated arcade action.

The fundamentals remain unmistakably NBA Jam. Matches are fast, physical and completely uninterested in realistic basketball simulation. Players shove opponents to the floor, launch themselves into impossible dunks, hit spectacular shots and catch fire after scoring three consecutive baskets. There are no fouls or out-of-bounds violations to slow the action down, and the famous commentary remains an essential part of the game's personality.

Tournament Edition significantly expands the roster, allowing teams to choose from several players rather than being restricted to a single pair. Substitutions can be made between quarters, while individual players have different ratings for attributes such as speed, three-point shooting, dunking and defense. Injuries and fatigue add another reason to rotate the lineup rather than simply choosing the same two stars for every quarter.

The new modes push the arcade mentality even further. Hot Spots can award unusually high-value baskets from specific areas of the court, while collectible power-ups temporarily grant advantages such as unlimited turbo, increased speed, improved shooting or spectacular Super Jams. Juice Mode can accelerate the entire game, while Tournament Mode removes the more extravagant bonuses and cheats for players who prefer a more straightforward competition.

The PlayStation conversion arrived in North America in 1995, with the European release following in 1996. Ported by Iguana UK and published by Acclaim, it belongs to the later generation of NBA Jam conversions that could reproduce much more of the arcade game's audiovisual character than the earlier cartridge versions.

One of the most obvious improvements is player scaling. Basketball players grow larger as they approach the foreground and shrink toward the opposite side of the court, reproducing an effect that was missing from the Genesis and Super Nintendo editions. The digitized heads are also much more recognizable, giving the players a closer resemblance to their real NBA counterparts during actual gameplay.

Sound is another major advantage. The PlayStation version offers clear stereo audio and a much broader range of Tim Kitzrow's commentary, including spoken player names. Combined with the familiar sneaker squeaks, impacts, crowd noise and emphatic calls after spectacular plays, it brings the home experience noticeably closer to the atmosphere of the arcade machine.

The roster was updated for this release and contains more than 120 NBA players, alongside Rookie and All-Star teams and the usual assortment of hidden characters and secret modes. Four-player support is available through the PlayStation Multitap, which is especially important for a game whose chaotic multiplayer matches have always been one of its greatest strengths. Progress can also be stored on a memory card rather than relying entirely on passwords.

The conversion is not perfect. Its biggest problem is loading. Pauses occur when entering matches and between quarters, interrupting a game whose appeal depends heavily on maintaining a relentless pace. They are not disastrous, but after playing cartridge versions or the arcade original, having the action repeatedly stop for CD access is difficult not to notice.

There are also small audiovisual differences that prevent it from being a completely exact reproduction of the coin-op, and the sprite scaling is not always as clean as it could be. Nevertheless, the game itself runs smoothly and retains the responsive controls, speed and exaggerated physicality that matter far more than minor graphical discrepancies.

Having covered NBA Jam and Tournament Edition across so many systems, the PlayStation version stands out as one of the conversions that finally had enough hardware behind it to reproduce most of what made the arcade game special rather than merely approximate it. Earlier versions could still be excellent games in their own right, but compromises in sprite detail, scaling and commentary were unavoidable. Here, those gaps are much smaller.

The loading times stop it from being the effortless arcade replacement it might otherwise have been, and other 32-bit versions can make a legitimate claim to even greater faithfulness. Even so, NBA Jam Tournament Edition on PlayStation is an excellent home version: fast, responsive, visually strong and packed with enough players, secrets and options to make an already outstanding arcade formula even more substantial.
